essentialQuestion.source: How do apps choose what we see, and why does that matter for a community?

learningGoal.source: Explain how a feed chooses posts, how that can help people discover things, why it matters for what a community knows before a vote, and what the evidence says.

warmUp.question.source: Why do you think some posts get shared much more than others?

evidence.label.source: Fictional example created for this lesson.

evidence.question.source: Which posts got shared most? How are Ravi's and Lena's feeds different, and how did Lena's help her?

evidence.cards.0.title.source: Posts in Maplebrook in the week of the town vote

evidence.cards.0.rows.0.0.source: “SHOCKING. The vote has moved to Friday. Share this now.” No name and no link.

evidence.cards.0.rows.1.0.source: Town election office: “The vote is on Saturday, from 9 to 5, at the town hall.”

evidence.cards.0.rows.2.0.source: Maplebrook Fact Check: “False. The vote has not moved. It is still on Saturday.”

evidence.cards.0.rows.3.0.source: A funny video of a goat walking into the library

evidence.cards.1.cases.0.body.source: Ravi watched a lot of football videos last month. This week, his feed showed him eight posts about the new sports field and one post about the new library.

evidence.cards.1.cases.1.body.source: Lena liked many posts about books. This week, her feed showed her seven posts about the new library and two posts about the sports field. It also suggested a free video lesson on how to write a story, which she had been looking for.

read.sections.0.heading.source: Your feed is chosen for you

read.sections.0.text.source: People post far more than anyone could see, so many apps use an algorithm to choose what goes in your feed. An algorithm is a set of steps a computer follows. It learns from what you watched, liked or skipped before. Then it guesses what you will want to see. Apps aim for different things. Some count how long you watch, and some also ask people if they were happy with what they saw. A feed can be very useful. It can help you discover a skill, a song or local news you would never have found. In the made-up town of Maplebrook, Lena liked posts about books, and her feed found her a free video lesson on writing stories. Ravi watched many football videos, so his feed showed him mostly posts about the new sports field.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: People post more than you could ever see. So many apps use an algorithm. An algorithm is a set of steps for a computer. It picks posts from what you watched before. Apps aim for different things. Some count how long you watch. Some ask if you liked it. A feed can help you find new things, like a skill or local news. In made-up Maplebrook, Lena likes books. Her feed found her a free lesson on stories. Ravi watches football. His feed shows him posts about the new sports field.

read.sections.1.heading.source: Feeds and what a town knows

read.sections.1.text.source: Each feed is chosen for one person. So two neighbours can see very different posts about the same town, as Ravi and Lena did before Maplebrook's vote. This matters for public life. To take part in an election, people need some shared, correct facts, such as the day of the vote. A rumour can spread fast. In 2018, researchers at MIT in the United States published a study of about 126,000 news stories shared on Twitter from 2006 to 2017. False stories spread further and faster than true ones. People did most of the sharing, not robot accounts. The study looked at what people shared on one site, so it did not show that feeds or AI caused the spread.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: Each feed is chosen for one person. So two neighbours can see different posts about the same town. Ravi and Lena did before the vote. In an election, people need the same true facts. One is the day of the vote. A rumour can spread fast. In 2018, MIT researchers in the US studied news stories on Twitter. The stories were from 2006 to 2017. False stories spread faster than true ones. People shared them, not only robots. The study looked at what people shared on one site. It did not show that feeds or AI caused this.

read.sections.2.heading.source: What the evidence says, and what helps

read.sections.2.text.source: Some people worry that feeds put each of us in a filter bubble, where we only see one side. But in 2022, a review of many studies by the Reuters Institute at the University of Oxford found that real filter bubbles are less common than many people think. People's own choices about what to follow also matter. A European Union law, in full use since 2024, says that very large apps must explain how their feeds choose posts. They must also offer a feed that isn't based on what they know about you. Apps change often, so a study from a few years ago may not describe them today. You can help as well: follow different sources, share the official notice and check before you share.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: Some people worry about a filter bubble. In a bubble, you only see one side. But in 2022, researchers looked at many studies. They found that real bubbles are less common than people think. What people choose to follow matters too. Since 2024, very big apps in the European Union must explain their feeds. They must offer another kind too. Apps change, so old studies may not fit them today. You can help. Follow different sources. Share the true notice. Check before you share.

read.glossary.0.definition.source: A set of steps a computer follows to do a job.

read.glossary.0.example.source: An algorithm chose the posts in Ravi's feed.

read.glossary.1.definition.source: The list of posts and videos an app shows you.

read.glossary.1.example.source: Lena's feed showed her many posts about the library.

read.glossary.2.definition.source: A story that people pass on without knowing if it is true.

read.glossary.2.example.source: The rumour said the vote had moved to Friday.

read.glossary.3.definition.source: A time when people vote to choose something together.

read.glossary.3.example.source: Maplebrook held an election to choose a library or a sports field.

read.glossary.4.definition.source: When a feed shows you only one side of things.

read.glossary.4.example.source: If Ravi only saw sports field posts, he would be in a filter bubble.

write.prompt.source: Ravi and Lena live in the same town, but they saw different posts before the vote. Explain why. Then say one thing that could help everyone in Maplebrook get the correct facts.

write.sentenceStarters.0.source: Ravi and Lena saw different posts because ...

write.sentenceStarters.1.source: This matters before a vote because ...

write.sentenceStarters.2.source: One thing that could help is ...

write.example.source: Ravi and Lena saw different posts because the algorithm guesses from what each of them liked before. Ravi watched football videos. So he saw mostly posts about the sports field. Lena liked books, so she saw mostly posts about the library. This matters before a vote because everyone needs the correct facts, like the day of the vote. One thing that could help is to share the election office's notice. It is correct, but it was shared only 60 times.

speak.partnerTask.source: Talk with your partner. How did Lena's feed help her? What might Ravi's feed not show him before the vote? Take turns, then agree on one way to see more than one side.

speak.independentTask.source: Say out loud what an algorithm does in a feed. Give one way it can help a community and one way it can cause problems before a vote.

watch.why.source: A short news video made for young people that explains how an algorithm chooses what you see.

watch.beforeQuestion.source: Who do you think chooses what you see when you scroll?

watch.afterQuestion.source: Why might a feed try to keep you watching?

watch.summary.source: This short news video for young people explains social media algorithms. An algorithm is a set of instructions that tells a computer program what to do. On many apps, the algorithm decides which posts you see and in what order. It also decides which posts you don't see. So when you scroll, you might think you are seeing everything. In fact, someone built a system that chooses for you. How does it choose? It tries to show you posts that will keep you interested, so you keep scrolling. Experts in the video say this isn't always a good thing. Your feed is carefully chosen. It is not a full view of the world. Knowing how your feed is chosen can help you think about what you see.

watch.keyPoints.0.source: An algorithm is a set of instructions for a computer.

watch.keyPoints.1.source: On many apps, an algorithm chooses which posts you see, and which you don't.

watch.keyPoints.2.source: It tries to keep you watching, which isn't always good for you.

watch.contentNote.source: About 3 minutes (182 seconds, from YouTube's listing), Canadian English, from 2021. It names real apps (TikTok, YouTube and Instagram). The title and channel were confirmed with YouTube's oEmbed on 31 October 2026. The summary was written from CBC Kids News' own description of the video and its web page, not from watching it. Someone on the team must watch it before learners use it; learners can read the written summary instead.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: Elections and politics can be painful or dangerous topics for some learners. Keep the discussion on made-up Maplebrook. Never ask learners about elections, politics or votes in any country they have lived in, or how anyone in their family votes, and don't let a debate about real candidates or parties start; steer back to how feeds and rumours work.

educatorNotes.0.source: The research in section 2 is Vosoughi, Roy and Aral (Science, March 2018; MIT News, 8 March 2018, re-read 8 November 2026): about 126,000 cascades of news stories on Twitter, 2006 to 2017, tweeted over 4.5 million times by about 3 million people, each story judged true or false by six independent fact-checking organisations that agreed over 95% of the time. False news was 70% more likely to be retweeted, and true stories took about six times as long to reach 1,500 people; the gap held with bots removed. Its scope: one platform, those years, and stories that fact-checkers had investigated (contested stories, not all posts). It measured what people retweeted, not how a ranking algorithm chose posts, so it does not show that AI caused the spread; the authors say other platforms need separate study, and that they “cannot claim that novelty causes retweets”.

educatorNotes.1.source: Apps rank posts with different signals and aims; don't reduce them to one motive. For example, YouTube's help page lists watch and search history, subscriptions, likes, dislikes, “not interested” and satisfaction surveys (to understand satisfaction, “not just watch time”). Filter bubbles: the Reuters Institute's 2022 review (Ross Arguedas, Robertson, Fletcher and Nielsen) found echo chambers “much less widespread than is commonly assumed”, “no support for the filter bubble hypothesis”, and an important role for people's own choices (self-selection); research outside the United States is limited. The European rule is the Digital Services Act (Regulation (EU) 2022/2065): in force 16 November 2022, applying in full from 17 February 2024, and earlier to very large platforms (over 45 million monthly users in the EU), four months after the Commission designated them; they must explain the main settings of their recommender systems, offer one not based on profiling, and assess risks such as the manipulation of elections.

educatorNotes.2.source: Section 3's point that apps change matters: the study's years (2006 to 2017) predate today's feeds, and Twitter is now called X. For discussion or on paper, put Ravi's and Lena's feeds side by side and ask what each friend sees, what each might miss, and how the election office's notice could reach both. There is no sorting task.
